title: Every Project Has a Constituency
summary: A development project succeeds or fails through people who do not work for you: contractors, consultants, officials, neighbours and community groups. Map them by power and interest, give each an owner and a plan, and you replace surprises with conversations. Cultural intelligence decides whether those conversations land.
body:
Mr Shabazz, nobody on your project is obliged to want it to succeed except you. A stakeholder plan is how you turn the people who can stop, slow, improve or support the project into known names with known interests, each with someone in your company responsible for the relationship.

Recall

Q. What is the first of the four integrity controls?

A. Know your counterparty: identify every investor, agent, partner and buyer, including the beneficial owners behind any chain of companies.

Q. What must investor reporting do after an offering, in concept?

A. Report results and material events honestly and on time, against what the offering documents promised, without misleading omissions.

Q. When you defend a structure chart to an auditor, what must every box be able to show?

A. Substance: why it exists, who decides there, what it owns and how money flows through it, supported by contemporaneous records.

Why this matters

A building is approved by authorities, priced by contractors, designed by consultants, financed by lenders and lived beside by neighbours. Each of them has interests that only partly overlap with yours. Most project delays that look technical, a stalled permit, a sudden claim, an appeal, a utility that will not connect, are relationship failures that arrived late. Projects that manage stakeholders well do not avoid disagreement. They hear it early, while it is cheap to act on.

This week is about those relationships: contractors and consultants, whom you pay; authorities, whom you cannot pay; and communities, whom you cannot instruct. Today is the frame. REGA joins on the regulatory side, and on Day 4 we compare how two systems treat consultation.

Mapping who matters

In plain English: list everyone who can affect the project or is affected by it, then sort them by how much they can affect it and how much they care.

The professional framing is a stakeholder map, often drawn as a power-interest grid. Power is the ability to change the outcome: an approval authority has high power, a neighbour with a right of appeal has some, a passer-by has none. Interest is how much the person cares. The grid gives four quadrants and four strategies. High power, high interest: manage closely and involve early. High power, low interest: keep satisfied and never surprise. Low power, high interest: keep informed and listen, because interest becomes power through petitions, media and politics. Low power, low interest: monitor.

A worked example, hypothetical. A developer plans a 60-unit apartment building beside a school. The planning authority and the utility are high power. The parents' association is high interest and, through its councillor, gaining power. The construction contractor is high power and high interest during the build. The bakery next door is low power and very high interest, because construction access will block its loading bay for months. Ignore the bakery, and the bakery will become the story at the council hearing.

Say that out loud now.

Every name on my map has an owner in my company and a next conversation on the calendar.

From map to register

A map is a picture; a stakeholder register is the working tool. For each stakeholder it records the interest in their own words, what they can do to the project, what they need from you, the person in your company who owns the relationship, the agreed way of communicating and the date of the next contact. Commitments you make go in it too, because a promise made by a site manager to a neighbour is a promise made by your company.

A second worked example, hypothetical. During excavation, the register shows a commitment to the bakery: no deliveries blocking its bay between 6 and 9 in the morning. In month 3 a concrete pour is scheduled for 7. The superintendent checks the register, moves the pump to the other side, and phones the bakery the day before. Total cost: one phone call and a slightly longer hose run. The alternative is a complaint to the authority, a stop-work visit and a hostile neighbour for two years.

The people you pay are stakeholders too

Beginners think of stakeholders as outsiders: neighbours, officials, activists. Your contractors and consultants belong on the map as well, because their interests diverge from yours at predictable moments. A contractor's interest is margin and cash flow, which peaks when it prices changes and bills early. A consultant's interest is scope and fee, which peaks when the brief is vague. An authority's interest is compliance and political safety, which peaks before an election or after a failure elsewhere.

Knowing those moments lets you act before them. Agree the change process before the first change. Write the consultant's scope so that what is excluded is as clear as what is included. Brief the authority's staff early on anything novel, so that the first time they see your unusual design is not at the counter with a queue behind you. The professional word for this is alignment: arranging the work so that each party's own interest pulls in the same direction as yours for as long as possible.

A practical test: for each paid stakeholder, write one sentence finishing the phrase, they make more money when. If the answer is when the project goes wrong for me, you have found the contract clause, the incentive or the reporting line that needs work.

Cultural intelligence

Cultural intelligence is the ability to read and adapt to how different groups communicate, decide and build trust. It is not stereotyping. It is asking, for each stakeholder, four questions. How directly do they say no? Who decides, and who must be consulted first? How much relationship must exist before business? And what does a commitment of time mean to them?

Across the places you may work, general norms differ, and individuals differ more. In some Canadian municipal settings, process is formal and written, and a meeting without a written follow-up barely happened. In some Guyanese settings, personal relationships and respect for seniority may carry more weight, and an early courtesy visit may matter more than a well-drafted letter. Treat these as hypotheses to test with local advisers, never as rules about people.

How the best do it

Large contractors and infrastructure owners appoint a named community liaison for major projects, publish a construction schedule of noisy and disruptive work in advance, run a complaints line with a response time they report on, and review the stakeholder register at every monthly project meeting alongside cost and schedule. A small developer can copy the core: one register, one owner per relationship, and a standing agenda item.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: community contributions may or may not be deductible or capitalised, depending on their form; verify against the primary source. Liability: promises to neighbours can become enforceable undertakings; write down what you mean. Banking: lenders discount projects with live opposition or appeals. Governance: decide who may make commitments to authorities and communities on the company's behalf. Estate: a development company's reputation in a town is part of what heirs inherit. Exit: buyers pay more for a building its neighbours accept.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is the low-power, high-interest stakeholder you never met, who becomes powerful at the worst moment. The control is a register reviewed monthly, with a named owner and a next contact for every high-interest party.

The beginner's mistake

Treating stakeholder engagement as a public relations task to begin after approval. The useful conversations happen before the design is fixed, while you can still change something.

Callback

In Week 3, Kema taught incentives and influence. Stakeholder management is applied incentive analysis: each party acts on what it is rewarded for, and your plan works only when you know what that is for each name on the map.

Recap

Map stakeholders by power and interest, turn the map into a register with owners, commitments and next contacts, and read each group with cultural intelligence rather than assumptions.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: Grenfell Tower and the residents whose warnings went unheard.
checklist: I list everyone who can affect or is affected by the project.
I place each stakeholder on a power-interest grid.
I keep a stakeholder register with interests, owners, commitments and next contacts.
I record every promise made to a stakeholder by anyone on my team.
I review the register at every monthly project meeting.
I test cultural assumptions with local advisers before acting on them.
I engage before the design is fixed, while change is still cheap.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every project has a constituency of people who do not work for me: contractors, consultants, authorities, neighbours and community groups. I map them on a power-interest grid. High power, high interest: manage closely. High power, low interest: keep satisfied. Low power, high interest: keep informed and listen, because interest turns into power. Low and low: monitor. The map becomes a stakeholder register, with each party's interest in their own words, what they can do to the project, an owner in my company, every commitment we have made, and the next contact date. I review it every month beside cost and schedule. I read each group with cultural intelligence: how directly they say no, who decides, how much relationship comes before business, and what a commitment of time means. Those are hypotheses to test, never stereotypes. And I engage before the design is fixed, while change is still cheap.
terms: Stakeholder — any person or group that can affect a project or is affected by it.
Power-interest grid — a map placing each stakeholder by their ability to change the outcome and how much they care, which sets the engagement strategy.
Cultural intelligence — the ability to read and adapt to how different groups communicate, decide and build trust, without stereotyping.

hostile.q: Your approval hearing is next month. Who in the community is going to speak against you, and what will they say?
hostile.a: I can tell you from our register. The parents' association is concerned about traffic at drop-off; we have agreed delivery hours and a revised entrance, and their chair has seen the plan. The bakery next door is concerned about loading access during construction; we have committed in writing to keep its bay clear in the mornings. The one group we have not met is the residents' association two streets over, and we have a meeting with them next week.

title: Grenfell Tower: The Warnings Nobody Owned
summary: On 14 June 2017 a fire at Grenfell Tower in London killed 72 people, spreading through cladding installed in a recent refurbishment. The public inquiry's final report in 2024 found failures across manufacturers, contractors, regulators and the building's owner and manager, including a long pattern of residents' concerns being dismissed. Seven steps, with Cole on accountability.
body:
Grenfell Tower is remembered for its cladding, and rightly. But part of the inquiry's story is a stakeholder failure: the people who lived in the building raised safety concerns for years, and the organisations responsible treated them as difficult tenants rather than as witnesses to risk.

Recall

Q. What is a power-interest grid?

A. A map of stakeholders by their ability to change the outcome and how much they care, which sets whether you manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed or monitor.

Q. What is Rule 72?

A. Never let anyone pay for a public decision on your behalf; every intermediary must show visible work, be paid into their own account at a defensible price, and be checked before engagement.

Q. In investor reporting, why does an omission matter as much as a false statement?

A. Because leaving out a material fact can make what was said misleading, which can ground the same claims as an outright untruth.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is the hardest case in the course to study coldly, and we should not pretend otherwise. Seventy-two people died. I have kept to facts that are widely established in the public record and in the inquiry's reports, and I describe the findings in general terms. Before you cite any finding in a meeting, read the report itself. Cole sits with me today because the inquiry's central question was accountability: who was responsible, and why responsibility spread so thin that nobody acted.

1. Timeline

Grenfell Tower was a 24-storey residential tower in North Kensington, London, owned by the local authority, the Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea, and managed for it by a tenant management organisation. A refurbishment completed in 2016 added new external cladding and insulation. Before and during the works, residents, some organised in an action group, raised concerns about fire safety and about how the building was managed. On the night of 14 June 2017 a fire that began in a flat spread up and across the outside of the building, and 72 people died. A public inquiry was established. Its first-phase report, on the night itself, was published in October 2019. Its final report was published in September 2024.

2. Key decisions

The inquiry examined many decisions, and Cole would caution against reducing them to one. For this week's subject three kinds matter. Choices of cladding and insulation products, made through a design and procurement chain in which each party relied on others for safety. Decisions by the building's owner and manager about how to respond to residents' complaints. And, over many years before, decisions by government and regulators about how building safety was tested and enforced.

3. Assumptions

The assumptions that recur in the inquiry's account are familiar ones. That someone else in the chain had checked the safety of the materials. That a product's marketing claims and certificates meant it was safe in this use. That compliance with guidance was the same as safety. And, on the relationship side, that residents raising alarms were a management problem to be contained rather than people who might be right.

4. Incentives

Cost and programme pressure on the refurbishment pushed toward cheaper options. Manufacturers had commercial reasons to present their products favourably, and the inquiry was severe about the conduct of some of them. Organisations managing the building had incentives to protect their reputation and to treat criticism as hostility. Nobody in the chain was rewarded for slowing down to answer a resident's question about fire.

Say that out loud now.

A complaint about safety is evidence, not noise.

5. Warning signs ignored

Residents raised concerns about fire safety and building management before the fire, including in public writing by an action group, and the inquiry described a relationship marked by distrust in which such concerns were not taken seriously. Across the wider industry, earlier fires in other countries and in the United Kingdom had shown how external wall systems could spread fire. Each of these was available to people with the power to act.

6. Point of no return

There is no single moment, and it would be dishonest to invent one. For a developer the useful framing is this: the last cheap point to change the outcome was before the cladding was specified and installed, when a question about the fire behaviour of the whole wall system could have been answered by testing and expert review. Once it was on the building, the remaining controls were fire safety management and the response to residents' concerns.

7. Root cause

The inquiry's findings are wide, and they include dishonesty by some product manufacturers and failures by regulators and government as well as by the contractors, consultants, owner and manager. For this week the root cause to carry away is the stakeholder one: responsibility for safety was spread across many parties, each assuming another held it, and the people with the most direct knowledge of the building's daily risks, its residents, had no route that forced an answer.

Cole's view: owning the warning

From an audit view, the question is always who owned the risk. A complaint log that records concerns but assigns no owner, no investigation and no written response is not a control; it is a record of notice. And notice matters, because once an organisation has been told of a risk, failing to act on it is judged differently. For your projects that means one practical rule: every safety concern, from a resident, a tradesperson or a neighbour, goes to a named person, gets investigated, and receives a written answer, and a pattern of concerns goes to the board.

Designing a route that forces an answer

You will own buildings with residents, tenants or guests, and you will build beside neighbours. Build the concern route before you need it. It has four parts. First, an intake anyone can use without knowing your organisation chart: a phone number, an email address and a notice in the lobby or on the site hoarding. Second, triage within a set number of days by a person with authority to spend money, with safety concerns separated from service complaints so they cannot be lost among them. Third, investigation by someone competent, a fire engineer for a fire concern, not a property manager. Fourth, a written answer to the person who raised it, saying what was found and what was done, and a quarterly summary to the board showing patterns.

Measure the route the way you measure a schedule: how many concerns came in, how fast each was triaged, how many were investigated, how many were answered. A route with no numbers is a route nobody is watching.

The biggest risk

For a small developer, the risk is assuming that the code, the product certificate and the consultants together have made the building safe, and that anyone who disagrees is being difficult. The control is Rule 73, plus an independent fire engineering review of any external wall system. Professional sign-off required: fire protection engineering.

The beginner's mistake

Measuring stakeholder relations by how quiet the complaints are. A quiet complaints log can mean safety, or it can mean people have given up telling you.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught hostile questions: acknowledge, bridge, answer. Residents' safety questions deserve the same structure, with one change: the answer must be investigated before it is given. Acknowledging a concern and then bridging away from it is exactly the habit this case warns against.

Recap

Grenfell's fire spread through an external wall system installed in a recent refurbishment. Among the inquiry's many findings was a long pattern of residents' concerns being dismissed by the organisations responsible. The stakeholder lesson is that the people closest to a building's risks need a route that forces an answer.

Rule 73: Treat every safety concern raised by the people who live in, work on or neighbour a building as evidence to be investigated and answered in writing, never as a relationship problem to be managed.

Next: Sage on The Money: how stakeholders move cost, time and value.
checklist: I route every safety concern to a named person with a deadline to respond.
I answer every safety concern in writing after investigating it.
I report patterns of concerns to the board, not only individual cases.
I commission independent fire engineering review of external wall systems.
I never treat a product certificate as proof of safety in my specific use.
I give residents and site workers a reporting route that reaches decision makers.
I treat a quiet complaints log as a question, not a reassurance.
head: Field checklist
speak: Grenfell Tower was a 24-storey residential block in London. A refurbishment completed in 2016 added new cladding and insulation. On 14 June 2017 a fire spread up the outside of the building and 72 people died. The public inquiry reported on the night in 2019 and published its final report in September 2024, finding failures across manufacturers, contractors, consultants, regulators, government and the building's owner and manager. Part of the story is a stakeholder failure: residents had raised fire safety and management concerns for years, and the inquiry described those concerns as not taken seriously. Responsibility was spread so thinly that each party assumed another held it, and the people closest to the risk had no route that forced an answer. Rule 73: treat every safety concern raised by those who live in, work on or neighbour a building as evidence to be investigated and answered in writing, never as a relationship problem to be managed.
terms: Public inquiry — a formal, independent investigation established by government to establish facts and make recommendations after a major event.
External wall system — the combination of cladding, insulation, cavities and fixings on a building's outside face, whose fire behaviour must be judged as a whole.
Notice — knowledge of a risk communicated to an organisation, after which failing to act is judged more severely.

hostile.q: Your tenants' association has written to you three times about the fire doors. What have you done about it?
hostile.a: Each letter is logged with a named owner. After the first, our fire safety consultant inspected every door on the two floors mentioned and found four that did not close fully; they were repaired within two weeks, and I wrote to the association with the report. After the second and third, we widened the inspection to the whole building and that report is due on a fixed date. I will send it to the association the day I receive it, and the pattern is on our board agenda.

rule: Rule 73: Treat every safety concern raised by the people who live in, work on or neighbour a building as evidence to be investigated and answered in writing, never as a relationship problem to be managed.

title: What a Stakeholder Is Worth in the Pro Forma
summary: Stakeholders rarely appear as a line in the pro forma, yet they move three of its biggest numbers: time to approval, construction price and exit value. Two worked examples price an appeal and a community investment, and a third shows how a contractor prices an owner's reputation. Warrick's Wealth Ledger closes.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a stakeholder who can delay your project by six months has a price in your pro forma whether you write it there or not. Write it there, and you can decide what it is worth spending to change it.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 73?

A. Treat every safety concern raised by people who live in, work on or neighbour a building as evidence to be investigated and answered in writing.

Q. What is the hidden cost of an investor failing a source-of-funds check at closing?

A. Delay: carrying cost, escalation and replacement equity raised under time pressure on worse terms, all far larger than the cost of an early check.

Q. Why does a structure need a documented flow of funds?

A. So that every movement of money between entities can be explained for tax, banking and audit purposes, with its character, whether dividend, interest, fee or return of capital, clear in advance.

Why this matters

A pro forma is a model of time as much as of money. Most stakeholder effects arrive through time: an approval that takes longer, a utility connection that slips, a neighbour's injunction during excavation, a contractor who stretches the programme to recover a bad price. Time costs money in three ways at once. Interest keeps running, costs keep escalating, and the return on your equity falls because the same money is tied up longer. That third effect is why delay hurts internal rate of return (IRR), the annualised return on the cash you put in, more than it hurts profit.

Worked example one: the price of an appeal

Hypothetical round numbers. A project costs 20,000,000 dollars and is worth 25,000,000 dollars on completion, a profit of 5,000,000 dollars, or 25 percent on cost. A residents' group appeals the approval and the appeal takes six months to resolve in your favour.

Step 1, carry. The land loan of 6,000,000 dollars at a hypothetical 8 percent costs about 240,000 dollars for six months. Other holding costs, insurance, taxes and site security, add a hypothetical 60,000 dollars. Carry: 300,000 dollars.

Step 2, escalation. The contractor's price is held for 90 days, then rises with an index. Suppose six months of escalation adds 2 percent to a 14,000,000 dollar construction contract: 280,000 dollars.

Step 3, consultants. Planning lawyers, expert witnesses and revised reports for the appeal: a hypothetical 120,000 dollars.

Total: 700,000 dollars. Profit falls from 5,000,000 to 4,300,000 dollars, from 25 percent to about 21 percent on the higher cost. And because the same equity now waits six months longer for that smaller profit, the IRR falls proportionally more. You won the appeal and still lost 700,000 dollars.

Say that out loud now.

Delay costs carry, escalation and return, all at once.

Worked example two: what engagement is worth

Now price the alternative. Before filing, the developer meets the residents' group and learns that their real concern is traffic at the school entrance. Moving the parking access to a side street and funding a crossing guard for the construction period costs a hypothetical 150,000 dollars. Suppose your planning adviser's judgment is that the chance of an appeal falls from 40 percent to 10 percent.

Expected cost without engagement: 40 percent of 700,000 dollars, which is 280,000 dollars. Expected cost with engagement: 10 percent of 700,000 dollars, or 70,000 dollars, plus the 150,000 dollars spent, which is 220,000 dollars. Engagement saves an expected 60,000 dollars, and it removes most of the chance of the worst case, which a lender cares about more than the average.

Notice what made the decision possible: a number on the appeal. Without it, the 150,000 dollars looks like a concession. With it, it looks like insurance priced below its risk. The probabilities are judgment, not data, and you should say so when you present them; but a stated judgment can be challenged and improved, and a silent one cannot.

Worked example three: what a contractor charges for you

Contractors are stakeholders who price your reputation directly. A contractor bidding for an owner it knows pays late, disputes every change and runs a slow decision process will add a premium for that risk, in its contingency, its margin or its general conditions. As a hypothetical, suppose that premium is 3 percent on a 14,000,000 dollar contract: 420,000 dollars. An owner with a record of paying on time, deciding changes within a week and meeting promptly may see that premium shrink or disappear, and may also get the best subcontractors, who choose which jobs to chase. Pricing in construction is commercial practice and no contractor will itemise this; you see it only in the spread of bids and in who chooses to bid at all.

Exit value: the neighbours are in the cap rate

At exit, a buyer prices the building's relationships as part of its risk. A residential building with an organised, hostile tenants' group, an open dispute with the neighbouring owner or an unresolved condition from the authority carries a risk a buyer will price, through a higher capitalisation rate or a lower bid. On a hypothetical net operating income (NOI) of 1,500,000 dollars, the difference between a 6.0 and a 6.25 percent cap rate is 25,000,000 against 24,000,000 dollars: a million dollars for a quarter of a point.

Where the numbers go in the model

Three places. First, the sources and uses, as a soft-cost line called community and stakeholder engagement: meetings, notices, a liaison's time, any agreed contributions. Name it, so it is spent deliberately and reported to the lender rather than buried in general contingency. Second, the schedule, as a stated assumption about time to approval with a range, for example base four months and downside ten, drawn from your planning adviser's view of comparable applications. Third, the risk register, as specific events with an owner, a probability and a priced consequence: appeal, neighbour injunction, utility refusal.

Then run the downside. Push the approval to the downside date and let the model recalculate carry, escalation and the interest reserve. If the project survives, you know how much patience you have. If it does not, you know before you buy the land, which is the only time that knowledge is cheap. A small developer who does this once will never again see a planning delay as bad luck. It becomes a variable with a price.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

For your personal balance sheet, a reputation for keeping commitments to stakeholders is an asset that compounds across projects: better bids, faster approvals and easier exits. It does not appear on a statement, so measure it indirectly. Track, project by project, the number of bidders, the time to approval and any disputes. If those numbers worsen, the asset is depreciating, and the cause will usually be a commitment you did not keep.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is leaving stakeholder risk out of the model because it is hard to quantify, so it is treated as zero. The control is a delay line in every pro forma, priced for carry, escalation and consultants, with stated probabilities for the main stakeholder events.

The beginner's mistake

Judging a community investment by its cost alone. A cost without the risk it changes is half a calculation. The second mistake is the reverse: promising contributions to win support without pricing them, then finding they were never in the budget and cannot be honoured.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman built stress tests and break-evens. Add a stakeholder delay to them: how many months of appeal can the project absorb before profit falls below your minimum, or the interest reserve runs out? That number tells you how much engagement is worth buying.

Recap

Stakeholders move time, price and exit value. A six-month appeal cost 700,000 dollars in the example; a 150,000 dollar engagement lowered the expected cost and the worst case; contractors price your reputation; buyers price the neighbours. Put a number on each and the decisions become clear.

Next: REGA on The Rules: consultation, notice and community agreements, comparing two systems.
checklist: I include a priced delay line in every pro forma.
I price carry, escalation and consultants separately for any delay.
I state my probabilities for stakeholder events and label them as judgment.
I compare engagement spending against the expected cost and the worst case it changes.
I track the number of bidders and time to approval across my projects.
I pay on time and decide changes promptly to lower contractors' risk premium.
I list unresolved stakeholder disputes as exit risks.
head: Field checklist
speak: Stakeholders rarely appear as a line in the pro forma, but they move time, price and exit value. In a hypothetical example, a six-month appeal on a 20,000,000 dollar project cost 300,000 dollars of carry, 280,000 of escalation and 120,000 of consultants: 700,000 dollars, taking profit from 25 to about 21 percent on cost, and IRR down more because the equity waited longer. Then I price the alternative. A 150,000 dollar change that addressed the residents' real concern, traffic, lowered the chance of appeal from 40 to 10 percent: expected cost 220,000 against 280,000, and far less chance of the worst case. Contractors price my reputation as an owner into their bids. Buyers price the neighbours into the cap rate; a quarter point on 1,500,000 dollars of NOI is a million dollars. So I put a delay line in every model and price engagement against the risk it changes.
terms: Internal rate of return (IRR) — the annualised return on the cash invested, which falls with delay because the same money is tied up longer.
Escalation — the rise in construction prices over time, often passed to the owner through an index clause after a price-hold period.
Expected cost — the probability of an event multiplied by its cost, used to compare options that change the probability.

hostile.q: You are spending 150,000 dollars on a side-street entrance nobody required. Why should the lender fund it?
hostile.a: Because it lowers the lender's risk more than it costs. An appeal would delay us six months and cost about 700,000 dollars, with the interest reserve absorbing much of it. Our planning adviser's judgment is that addressing the traffic concern cuts the chance of an appeal from 40 to 10 percent. The expected cost falls, and the severe case, which is the one you size against, becomes much less likely. I can show you the calculation and the adviser's note.

title: Notice, Consultation and the Promises You Sign
summary: The law governs stakeholders through four instruments: notice and hearing requirements in planning, consultation inside environmental assessment, private rights of neighbours, and agreements you sign with communities and authorities. Week 73 is an odd week, so Two Systems compares how Canada and Guyana approach consultation, in concept.
body:
Most stakeholder law does not tell you to be nice. It tells you who must be told, who must be heard, what neighbours can stop, and which of your promises a court will enforce. Know those four, and you know where engagement stops being optional.

Recall

Q. Why does delay hurt IRR more than it hurts profit?

A. Because carry and escalation reduce profit while the same equity is tied up longer, so the annualised return falls on both counts.

Q. Name the four legal regimes behind integrity.

A. Anti-money laundering, beneficial ownership transparency, anti-bribery and sanctions.

Q. What is permanent establishment, in concept, and why does it matter to a structure?

A. A fixed place of business or a dependent agent through which a foreign company can become taxable in a country; it matters because activity on the ground can create tax presence the structure chart did not intend.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, engagement that is optional can be planned for your convenience. Engagement that is required has a form, a timetable and a consequence for getting it wrong, often that the approval itself can be challenged. You need to know which is which before you set a schedule. Everything below is concept, not jurisdictional conclusion. Verify any requirement, timeline or threshold against the primary source and with local planning counsel before you rely on it.

Instrument one: notice and hearing in planning

In plain English: before some approvals are granted, the public must be told and given a chance to speak.

The professional framing: planning legislation commonly requires that certain applications, such as rezonings, variances and some subdivisions, be publicly notified, by signs on site, mailed notice to nearby owners or published notice, and that a public meeting or hearing be held before a decision. Many systems also give defined parties a right to appeal. The legal significance is procedural: a decision made without the required notice may be open to challenge, whatever its merits.

A worked example, hypothetical. A variance application requires mailed notice to owners within a defined distance. The developer's consultant uses an outdated ownership list, and one owner is missed. The variance is granted. The missed owner learns of it from the hoarding and challenges the decision for defective notice. Even if the variance is later re-granted, the delay runs months. The control is cheap: confirm the notice list against the current land registry and keep proof of every notice served.

Instrument two: consultation inside environmental assessment

Larger or sensitive projects can require an environmental impact assessment, often called an EIA: a formal study of a project's effects on the environment and on people, with measures to avoid or reduce them. Many EIA regimes require public consultation at defined stages, publication of the study, and consideration of submissions before a decision. Some impose conditions requiring ongoing engagement during construction and operation. Whether your project triggers an assessment depends on its type, size and location; ask early, because the assessment timetable often sets the critical path.

Say that out loud now.

Who must be told, who must be heard, what neighbours can stop, and which promises a court will enforce.

Instrument three: neighbours' private rights

Separate from public approvals, neighbours have private law rights. In common law systems these commonly include a claim in nuisance for unreasonable interference with the use of land, through noise, dust or vibration; rights of support, so that excavation must not undermine adjoining land; and protections against trespass, for example by a crane jib swinging over a neighbour's air space. A court can award damages and sometimes an injunction stopping the work. That makes a neighbour with a strong private claim a high-power stakeholder no approval can neutralise. The usual answer is a negotiated agreement: a licence for crane oversail, a pre-construction condition survey of the neighbour's building, and monitoring of vibration and movement.

Instrument four: the agreements you sign

Developers often make promises to win support: a community benefit agreement with a neighbourhood group, a development agreement with the municipality, a letter to a school about delivery hours. A community benefit agreement is a contract between a developer and community parties setting out benefits, such as local hiring, public space or funding, in exchange for support or non-opposition. Whether such promises are enforceable, by whom and how, depends on their form and the governing law. Two lessons follow. Draft only what you will deliver, with measurable terms and an end date. And keep a single register of every commitment, because a promise in a site manager's email can be cited back to you later. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer qualified in the governing law.

A second worked example, hypothetical. To win a neighbourhood association's support, a developer writes that the project will hire locally and fund a park. Two years later the association asks for the park, a 300,000 dollar item never put in the budget, and points to the letter. The developer's lawyer reads it and finds no amount, no date and no condition, which makes it arguable, expensive to fight and impossible to ignore politically. Compare a well-drafted version: the developer will contribute 100,000 dollars toward park improvements, payable at occupancy, conditional on final approval being granted without appeal; and will advertise construction vacancies through a named local employment office for the duration of the works. Every term is measurable, every obligation has a trigger, and the cost is in the pro forma.

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

This is a conceptual comparison only. Verify against primary source before relying on any of it.

Canada: land-use planning is largely provincial legislation administered by municipalities, which typically sets notice and public meeting requirements for rezonings and similar approvals, with appeal routes that vary by province. Federal and provincial environmental assessment regimes apply to some projects. Distinctively, Canadian constitutional law recognises a duty on the Crown to consult, and where appropriate accommodate, Indigenous peoples when contemplated government action may adversely affect asserted or established Aboriginal or treaty rights; procedural parts of that duty can be delegated to project proponents in practice. A developer whose project needs an approval that triggers the duty may find consultation on the critical path [unverified — confirm independently].

Guyana: planning approvals involve the national housing and planning authority and local authorities, and environmental legislation administered by the Environmental Protection Agency requires assessment, including public consultation, for projects that may significantly affect the environment. Guyanese legislation also recognises titled Amerindian village lands with village councils exercising defined powers over activities on those lands [unverified — confirm independently].

The comparison for you: both systems place consultation inside approval processes, so the form and timing matter legally, not only commercially. Both recognise Indigenous land interests, through different legal routes. And in both, local practice, who to visit first and in what order, carries weight the statute does not describe. Ask local counsel and a local planning adviser before you set a timetable.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is defective process: an approval granted on incomplete notice or skipped consultation, which survives until someone challenges it at the worst moment. The control is a process checklist built with planning counsel, with proof of every step filed.

The beginner's mistake

Believing that a granted approval is safe from challenge. Until appeal periods have run and process has been checked, an approval is a strong position, not a certainty.

Callback

In Week 32, Pax and REGA covered entitlements: pre-application, conditions, variances, appeals and development agreements. Today adds the stakeholder view of the same machinery: each step in an entitlement is also a moment when someone outside your company gains a legal voice.

Recap

Four instruments: public notice and hearings, consultation within environmental assessment, neighbours' private rights, and the agreements you sign. Canada and Guyana both build consultation into approval and both recognise Indigenous land interests, by different legal routes.

Next: Marco on The Numbers: building an engagement budget and a delay model, step by step.
checklist: I confirm with planning counsel which notices and hearings each approval requires.
I check notice lists against the current land registry and keep proof of service.
I ask early whether the project triggers an environmental assessment.
I commission pre-construction condition surveys of adjoining buildings.
I negotiate crane oversail and access licences before work starts.
I draft community commitments with measurable terms and an end date.
I keep one register of every promise made to any stakeholder.
head: Field checklist
speak: Stakeholder law works through four instruments. Planning law requires notice and hearings for some approvals, and a decision made without proper notice can be challenged whatever its merits. Environmental assessment regimes often require consultation at defined stages and can set the critical path. Neighbours have private rights, in nuisance, support and against trespass, so a strong neighbour claim can stop work even with every approval in hand; the answer is a negotiated licence, a condition survey and monitoring. And the promises I sign, development agreements and community benefit agreements, may be enforceable, so I draft only what I will deliver, with measurable terms, and keep one register of every commitment. Canada and Guyana both build consultation into approvals and both recognise Indigenous land interests, by different routes. Every specific is jurisdictional, so I verify with local counsel before setting a timetable.
terms: Environmental impact assessment (EIA) — a formal study of a project's effects on the environment and people, often with required public consultation.
Nuisance — a private law claim for unreasonable interference with a neighbour's use and enjoyment of their land.
Community benefit agreement — a contract between a developer and community parties setting out benefits delivered in exchange for support.

hostile.q: A neighbour says your excavation will undermine her building. Your permits are in order. Why should you negotiate with her at all?
hostile.a: Because the permits answer the authority, not her private rights. If she has a valid claim in support or nuisance, a court could award damages or stop the work, and the delay would cost more than any agreement. So we have offered a pre-construction condition survey of her building, vibration and movement monitoring with agreed limits, and an engineer's review of our shoring design. That protects her building and our schedule at the same time.

title: Building the Engagement Budget and the Stakeholder Risk Line
summary: A worked calculation, step by step, with hypothetical round numbers: build a stakeholder engagement budget from its parts, then price three stakeholder risks as expected costs and a severe case, and compare the result with the contingency you carry. The output is two lines you can defend to a lender.
body:
Engagement is a work package like any other: it has quantities, rates and a total. Stakeholder risk is a set of events with probabilities and prices. Put both in the model, and you can show a lender exactly what you are spending to avoid what.

Recall

Q. What is a community benefit agreement?

A. A contract between a developer and community parties setting out benefits, such as local hiring or public space, delivered in exchange for support or non-opposition; enforceability depends on its form and the governing law.

Q. What is the difference between expected cost and the severe case?

A. Expected cost is probability times consequence, the average across outcomes; the severe case is the single bad outcome you must survive, which lenders size against.

Q. In repatriation, why does the character of a payment matter?

A. Because dividends, interest, fees and returns of capital can be taxed and withheld differently, so the same cash can carry different leakage depending on what it is called and what it really is.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a lender reading your budget will ask two questions about stakeholders. What are you spending, and on what? And what happens if it does not work? This lesson builds the answer to both, line by line, for a hypothetical 60-unit apartment project with a construction contract of 14,000,000 dollars and an 18-month build. Every rate and quantity is hypothetical and should be replaced with local figures before use.

Step 1: list the engagement work

Break engagement into work you can count, the same way a quantity surveyor breaks down a building.

  • A community liaison, part time, 2 days a week for 24 months, covering pre-application, approval and construction.
  • Public meetings: 4 before approval and 2 during construction, each with room hire, materials and staff time.
  • Notices and mailings: statutory notices plus a quarterly construction newsletter to 400 nearby addresses.
  • Pre-construction condition surveys of 3 adjoining buildings, with a follow-up survey at completion.
  • Vibration and movement monitoring during excavation and foundations, 6 months.
  • A complaints line and log, run by the liaison.

Step 2: price each line

Use hypothetical rates.

Liaison: 2 days a week is about 100 days a year; over 2 years, 200 days at 500 dollars a day is 100,000 dollars.

Meetings: 6 meetings at 4,000 dollars each, including staff and consultant attendance, is 24,000 dollars.

Notices and newsletters: 8 quarterly mailings to 400 addresses at 2 dollars each is 6,400 dollars; statutory notices, say 5,000 dollars. Total 11,400 dollars.

Condition surveys: 3 buildings at 3,000 dollars, twice, is 18,000 dollars.

Monitoring: 6 months at 5,000 dollars a month is 30,000 dollars.

Complaints line: included in the liaison's time, plus 1,600 dollars for a phone line and log.

Total engagement budget: 100,000 plus 24,000 plus 11,400 plus 18,000 plus 30,000 plus 1,600, which is 185,000 dollars.

Engagement budget: 185,000 dollars, about 1.3 percent of a 14,000,000 dollar construction contract. Name it as its own soft-cost line.

Say that out loud now.

Engagement has quantities, rates and a total, like any other work package.

Step 3: price the stakeholder risks

Now list the events that could still happen despite the engagement, with your adviser's judgment of probability and a priced consequence. Each consequence uses the delay arithmetic from Day 3: carry at a hypothetical 50,000 dollars a month on the land loan and holding costs, plus escalation and consultants.

Event A, appeal of the approval. Delay 6 months: carry 300,000 dollars, escalation 280,000 dollars, consultants 120,000 dollars. Consequence 700,000 dollars. Probability after engagement: 10 percent. Expected cost: 70,000 dollars.

Event B, neighbour injunction during excavation over vibration. Delay 2 months: carry 100,000 dollars, plus contractor standby claims of a hypothetical 150,000 dollars. Consequence 250,000 dollars. Probability with monitoring and an agreed limit: 5 percent. Expected cost: 12,500 dollars.

Event C, utility connection late because the authority's capacity review slips. Delay 3 months to occupancy: carry 150,000 dollars plus lost rent on 60 units at a hypothetical 1,500 dollars a month for 3 months, 270,000 dollars. Consequence 420,000 dollars. Probability: 20 percent. Expected cost: 84,000 dollars.

Total expected cost: 70,000 plus 12,500 plus 84,000, which is 166,500 dollars.

Step 4: find the severe case

Expected cost is an average and no project lives the average. A lender asks what you must survive. Suppose your severe case is two events together, the appeal and the utility delay: 700,000 plus 420,000 dollars, or 1,120,000 dollars. Test it against two things. Is it covered by contingency and the interest reserve? And does the project still clear your minimum profit if it happens? If contingency on this project is a hypothetical 5 percent of construction, 700,000 dollars, the severe case is 420,000 dollars larger than contingency. That is the number to discuss with your lender: covered by a sponsor commitment, by more equity, or by more work to reduce the probabilities.

Step 5: compare and decide

Lay the numbers side by side. Engagement spending: 185,000 dollars. Remaining expected stakeholder cost: 166,500 dollars. Severe case: 1,120,000 dollars against 700,000 dollars of contingency. The sensible next move is not to cut engagement but to attack Event C, the largest expected cost, with an early capacity request to the utility and a written confirmation of its timeline. If that halves the probability to 10 percent, expected cost on C falls to 42,000 dollars, and the severe case becomes less likely.

Step 6: rank the relationships, not only the risks

Money tells you which events matter. A simple score tells you which people to see first. Rate each stakeholder from 1 to 5 for power and 1 to 5 for interest, and multiply. The product, from 1 to 25, is a rough priority, not a measurement; its value is that it forces a decision and can be argued with.

Hypothetical scores. The planning authority: power 5, interest 3, priority 15. The utility: power 5, interest 2, priority 10. The parents' association: power 3, interest 5, priority 15. The neighbour on the excavation side: power 4, interest 5, priority 20. The bakery: power 2, interest 5, priority 10. The general contractor: power 4, interest 4, priority 16.

Two things stand out. The neighbour on the excavation side, not the authority, is the top relationship, because a private law claim gives her real power and the excavation gives her every reason to use it. And the utility, low on interest, is high on the money list from Step 3. A low-interest, high-power party is the one most likely to surprise you through indifference rather than hostility, which is why Event C carried the largest expected cost. Put both at the top of the liaison's calendar this month.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that the probabilities are written once and never revised, so the model goes on reporting comfort after the facts change. The control is to re-score each event at every monthly project meeting and to move the numbers when the register shows new information.

The beginner's mistake

Adding the expected costs and calling the total a contingency. Expected cost is an average. You carry contingency for the bad case, not the average one. The second mistake is false precision: quoting a probability to the decimal as if it were data. Say it is your adviser's judgment, give a range, and show how the answer moves across that range.

Callback

In Week 13, Sage built sources and uses and warned against hiding costs inside contingency. The engagement budget is the same discipline applied to people: give it its own line, so that it is spent deliberately and reported honestly rather than drawn from contingency until nothing is left.

Recap

Engagement priced from its parts came to 185,000 dollars. Three stakeholder events carried an expected cost of 166,500 dollars and a severe case of 1,120,000 dollars against 700,000 dollars of contingency, which points the next effort at the largest expected cost.

Next: REGA on The Room: the community meeting where the room is against you.
checklist: I break engagement into countable work and price each line.
I carry engagement as its own named soft-cost line.
I list stakeholder events with a probability, a priced consequence and an owner.
I calculate expected cost and a severe case separately.
I test the severe case against contingency and the interest reserve.
I direct effort at the largest expected cost first.
I re-score every event at each monthly project meeting.
head: Field checklist
speak: Engagement is a work package. For a hypothetical 60-unit project, a part-time liaison for two years at 500 dollars a day is 100,000 dollars; six meetings 24,000; notices and newsletters 11,400; condition surveys 18,000; vibration monitoring 30,000; a complaints line 1,600. Total 185,000 dollars, about 1.3 percent of a 14,000,000 dollar contract, carried as its own line. Then the risks. An appeal costing 700,000 at 10 percent is 70,000 expected. A neighbour injunction costing 250,000 at 5 percent is 12,500. A late utility costing 420,000 at 20 percent is 84,000. Expected total 166,500. But the lender sizes against the severe case: appeal plus utility, 1,120,000 dollars, against 700,000 of contingency. So the next effort goes to the largest expected cost, the utility, with an early capacity request, and every probability is re-scored at each monthly meeting.
terms: Engagement budget — the priced work of informing, consulting and protecting stakeholders, carried as its own soft-cost line.
Severe case — the specific combination of bad outcomes a project must survive, used to size contingency and lender protections.
Standby claim — a contractor's claim for the cost of idle labour and equipment when work is stopped for a reason it does not carry.

hostile.q: Your severe case is 1,120,000 dollars and your contingency is 700,000. Where does the other 420,000 come from?
hostile.a: Three answers, in order of preference. First, we are working to make it less likely: an early capacity request to the utility should cut that event's probability, and I will report the utility's written response. Second, if it still sits above contingency at closing, I will provide a sponsor commitment for the gap, capped and documented. Third, if neither satisfies you, we will increase the contingency in the budget and fund it with equity. I would rather agree the answer now than ask for a waiver later.

title: The Community Meeting When the Room Is Against You
summary: A hypothetical public meeting about a proposed 60-unit building beside a school, with a hostile room, a local councillor and a reporter. The lesson gives the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, when to stay silent, how to hold your state, and how cultural intelligence changes the same meeting in two places.
body:
A hostile community meeting is not a debate you win. It is an evidence-gathering session in which your job is to hear the real concerns, show you have heard them, commit only to what you will deliver, and leave the room with more people willing to keep talking than when you arrived.

Recall

Q. How do you calculate an engagement budget?

A. Break engagement into countable work, such as liaison days, meetings, notices, surveys and monitoring, price each at local rates, and total it as its own soft-cost line.

Q. Why can a neighbour stop work even when every permit is in order?

A. Because permits answer the authority, while the neighbour may have private law rights, such as support or nuisance, that a court can enforce with damages or an injunction.

Q. What should a beneficial ownership check do with a nominee?

A. Look through it to the principal on whose behalf it holds, and refuse the holding if the principal will not be named.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the scene is hypothetical. You are the developer of a 60-unit apartment building on a corner lot beside a primary school. It is a Tuesday evening in the school gym. About 80 residents have come. The local councillor is in the front row. A reporter from the local paper is at the back. Your planning consultant and your liaison are with you. The first speaker, a parent, says: you are going to put construction trucks past my children every morning for two years, and you have not asked one of us what we think.

The question behind the question

Most questions in a meeting like this have a second question underneath. The parent's real question is: will you protect my children, and can I trust you to keep your word? The councillor's silence is a question too: is this project going to cost me votes? The reporter's question is whether there will be a story. Answer the question underneath, and the one on the surface usually settles. Argue with the surface, and you lose all three.

The lines to say

  • Thank you for coming. I am here to listen first and answer second, and I will stay until the last question.
  • You are right that we should have spoken with parents earlier. We are doing it now, and here is what we heard from the two meetings we have held so far.
  • Here is what we have already changed: the site entrance moves to the side street, no deliveries between 7.30 and 9 in the morning or 2.30 and 4 in the afternoon on school days, and a paid traffic marshal at the corner during those hours.
  • Here is what I do not know yet, and when I will know it.
  • Our liaison's name and number are on the handout. Every concern you raise tonight goes in a register, and you will get a written reply within two weeks.

Say that out loud now.

I will listen first, commit only to what I will deliver, and put every concern in writing with a date for the answer.

The lines never to say

  • The project complies with every regulation. True, perhaps, and it answers a question nobody asked.
  • Change is always hard for people. That tells the room you think their concern is a feeling.
  • We will make sure there are no problems at all. A promise you cannot keep becomes the headline when you break it.
  • I cannot discuss that. If a matter is truly confidential, say why, in plain terms, and say when you can discuss it.
  • Anything aimed at the councillor or the reporter. Speak to the residents; the others are listening anyway.

When to stay silent

Stay silent through the first speaker's whole statement, even if it runs long and contains errors. Interrupting to correct a fact tells the room you value the fact more than the person. Note the errors and address them later, briefly and without triumph. Stay silent, too, after a resident tells a personal story, a child hit by a car years ago, a parent who cannot afford to move. Do not rush to a solution. A pause of a few seconds, then a plain acknowledgement, does more than any plan.

Cultural intelligence: the same meeting in two places

General norms are starting points to test with local advisers, never rules about people, and individuals vary widely.

In many Canadian municipal settings, a meeting like this tends to be formal and process-driven: residents expect a written record, a clear statement of the approval timeline, and answers that refer to the planning documents. Directness is common, and an open public challenge is not necessarily personal. Follow-up in writing is what makes the meeting count.

In some Guyanese community settings, the meeting may matter less than what happened before it. A courtesy visit to respected community figures, religious leaders or long-standing residents, before any public event, may be expected, and arriving without one can read as disrespect. Disagreement may be expressed more indirectly in public and more directly in private conversations afterwards, so the real feedback may come at the door rather than at the microphone. Ask your local adviser who should be visited first, in what order, and whether the meeting should be chaired by someone the community already knows.

A worked example: the commitment you can make

Midway through, a resident asks you to guarantee that no truck will ever use the school street. You cannot control every delivery driver in a city, and saying yes would be the line you will be quoted on when it fails. The answer that holds: we will route all site traffic by the side street, put that route in every subcontract with a penalty for breach, post the marshal at the corner during school hours, and publish the complaints line. If a truck uses the school street, call the line, and we will tell you within a day what we did about it. That is a commitment with a mechanism and a consequence, which is what trust is built from.

How to hold your state

A hostile room raises your heart rate before you know it has. Before you go in, while parked, take two or three slow breaths with a longer exhale, a practitioner habit for steadying yourself; check that with your doctor if breathing drills are new to you. In the room, stand rather than sit behind a table, speak more slowly than feels natural, and keep your hands visible and still. Reframe the anger as information you need: every angry statement is telling you what the register is missing. If you feel heat rising, slow down further and ask a clarifying question; it buys you time and shows you are listening.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is promising in the room to end the hostility, then failing to deliver, which converts a difficult meeting into a broken promise on the record. The control is to agree in advance, with your team, exactly what you are authorised to commit to that evening, and to defer everything else to a written reply with a date.

The beginner's mistake

Bringing a presentation. A slide deck tells the room you came to talk. Bring a one-page handout with the changes already made, the open questions and the liaison's contact, and spend the time listening.

Callback

In Week 5, Kema taught pace, pause and listening. This meeting is where those skills earn their keep: the slowest speaker in the room, who lets silence work and answers the question underneath, is usually the one who leaves with the most goodwill.

Recap

Listen first, answer the question underneath, commit only to what has a mechanism behind it, put every concern in writing with a date for the reply, and adapt the meeting to local norms through a trusted adviser.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap for the stakeholder week.
checklist: I agree in advance exactly what I may commit to in the room.
I listen to each speaker in full before responding.
I answer the question underneath the question.
I commit only to promises with a mechanism and a consequence.
I log every concern and promise a written reply by a stated date.
I ask a local adviser who to visit before the meeting and who should chair it.
I bring a one-page handout, not a slide deck.
head: Field checklist
speak: A hostile community meeting is not a debate. It is evidence gathering. I listen to each speaker in full, then answer the question underneath: will you protect my children, and can I trust your word. I say what we have already changed, what I do not know yet and when I will, and that every concern goes in a register with a written reply within two weeks. I never say we comply with every regulation, never call concern a feeling, never promise there will be no problems, and never play to the councillor or the reporter. When asked for a guarantee I cannot give, I give a commitment with a mechanism: a route written into every subcontract with a penalty, a marshal at the corner, and a complaints line answered within a day. I adapt the meeting to local norms through a trusted adviser, and I agree in advance exactly what I am authorised to commit to.
terms: Question behind the question — the underlying concern, often about safety or trust, that a surface question stands for.
Courtesy visit — an informal, early meeting with respected community figures before any public event, expected in some settings.
Commitment with a mechanism — a promise backed by a specific process and consequence, such as a contract penalty, rather than by intention alone.

hostile.q: You say you listen to residents. Why did you file your application before talking to a single parent?
hostile.a: Because we got the order wrong, and I will not defend it. We should have met parents before filing. Since then we have held two meetings and changed three things: the site entrance, delivery hours around school times and a traffic marshal. Tonight's concerns go into our register, and you will have written replies within two weeks. If any of them change the design, we will amend the application rather than argue it through.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 73 Review: Stakeholders, Promises and the People Next Door
summary: Six questions test the week: the power-interest grid, the register, Rule 73, the cost of delay, neighbours' private rights and safe commitments. A Red Pen drill finds the defects in a hypothetical letter to neighbours, and a two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: the people who do not work for you decide your timetable, so know each of them by name, give each an owner in your company, price what they can do, and promise only what you will deliver.

Recall

Q. What is the difference between a stakeholder's power and interest?

A. Power is the ability to change the project's outcome; interest is how much the stakeholder cares. A low-power, high-interest party can gain power through petitions, media and politics.

Q. What is the second regime of integrity law, after anti-money laundering?

A. Beneficial ownership transparency: requirements that companies know, record and sometimes disclose the natural persons who ultimately own or control them.

Q. Why should every box in a structure chart have a substance record?

A. Because tax authorities and banks test where decisions are really made and what each entity really does, and contemporaneous evidence is the only convincing answer.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is the week that separates developers who are surprised by their projects from developers who are not. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer. Then do the Red Pen without looking at the defects first; the habit you are building is reading your own team's letters with a stranger's eyes.

One more instruction. When you check your answers, look for the mechanism in each one. A stakeholder answer without an owner, a date or a consequence is an intention, and intentions are exactly what the people next door have learned not to trust.

The six questions

Question 1. What is a power-interest grid, and what are its four strategies?

Answer: A map of stakeholders by ability to change the outcome and how much they care. High power and high interest: manage closely. High power, low interest: keep satisfied. Low power, high interest: keep informed and listen. Low and low: monitor.

Question 2. What goes in a stakeholder register?

Answer: Each party's interest in their own words, what they can do to the project, what they need, the owner in your company, every commitment made to them, the agreed channel and the next contact date.

Question 3. What is Rule 73?

Answer: Treat every safety concern raised by the people who live in, work on or neighbour a building as evidence to be investigated and answered in writing, never as a relationship problem to be managed.

Question 4. How does a six-month appeal cost money three ways at once?

Answer: Carry keeps running, escalation raises the construction price, and the same equity waits longer for its return, so IRR falls faster than profit.

Question 5. Why can a neighbour stop work when every permit is in order?

Answer: Because permits answer the authority, while neighbours may have private law rights, such as support or nuisance, that a court can enforce with damages or an injunction.

Question 6. What makes a promise to a community safe to make?

Answer: Measurable terms, a trigger and an end date, a cost already in the pro forma, a mechanism and a consequence behind it, and an entry in the commitments register.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Marco framed every project as a constituency and turned the map into a register, with cultural intelligence as a set of questions rather than assumptions. Ford and Cole took Grenfell Tower, where residents' safety concerns found no route that forced an answer, giving Rule 73. Sage priced a six-month appeal at 700,000 dollars and showed why engagement can be cheap insurance. REGA mapped notice, consultation, neighbours' rights and signed promises, and compared Canada and Guyana. Marco built a 185,000 dollar engagement budget and a stakeholder risk line with a severe case. REGA ran the hostile community meeting.

Red Pen

Here is a hypothetical letter a site manager sent to neighbours before excavation. Find the defects before reading on.

Dear Neighbour, Work on the new building starts Monday. We comply with all regulations, so there is nothing to worry about. We guarantee there will be no damage to your property and no noise before 7 in the morning. Trucks will avoid the school street wherever possible. We will also be making a generous contribution to the park. If you have any issues, please contact the main office. Thank you for your patience. Site Manager.

The defects. First, the notice arrives on the eve of the work, too late for any concern to change anything, and it does not mention the condition survey that should have been offered beforehand. Second, compliance with regulations is offered as reassurance, which answers the authority, not the neighbour. Third, a guarantee of no damage is a promise nobody can keep and invites a claim for every crack; the right offer is a survey before and after, monitoring with agreed limits and a named route for concerns. Fourth, wherever possible is a commitment with no mechanism; the route should be in every subcontract with a penalty. Fifth, a generous contribution to the park has no amount, no date and no condition, and it was almost certainly not authorised or budgeted. Sixth, the main office is not a person; there is no named liaison, no phone number and no response time. Seventh, the site manager is making company commitments that should have been agreed in advance and entered in the commitments register.

A corrected version would arrive weeks earlier, offer a condition survey, give working hours and monitoring limits as facts, name the liaison with a phone number and a two-day response time, state the delivery route and how it is enforced, and say nothing about the park unless an agreement with a figure and a trigger already exists.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to an investor who asks, why are you spending money on neighbours who have no say in the approval? Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Because they do have a say, just not always in the approval. Neighbours can appeal some decisions, bring private claims that stop work, and shape what a future buyer pays. So we map every stakeholder by power and interest, give each one an owner in our team, and keep a register of every concern and every promise. We price what they can do to us: on this project an appeal would cost about 700,000 dollars, and our full engagement budget is 185,000. We promise only what we can deliver, with a mechanism behind it, and we answer every safety concern in writing. That keeps our timetable ours."

Score yourself. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you show that stakeholders have real power? Did you give one number for the risk and one for the spend? Did you finish inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is the promise made casually by someone on your team, in a letter, an email or a hallway, that the company never priced, never authorised and cannot keep. The control is one rule: no commitment to any stakeholder unless it is authorised in advance and entered in the register.

The beginner's mistake

Waiting for opposition to appear before engaging. By then the design is fixed, the schedule is set and every change costs money. The cheapest conversation is the earliest one.

Callback

In Week 48, Marco set up the owner's decision log and approval authorities. The commitments register is its outward-facing twin: the decision log records what the company decided, and the register records what the company promised to others. Both need the same discipline of authority and record.

Recap

Map by power and interest, run a register with owners and commitments, treat safety concerns as evidence, price stakeholder risk with expected costs and a severe case, respect neighbours' private rights and the process rules of approval, and promise only what has a mechanism behind it.

checklist: What is a power-interest grid, and what are its four strategies?
What goes in a stakeholder register?
What is Rule 73?
How does a six-month appeal cost money three ways at once?
Why can a neighbour stop work when every permit is in order?
What makes a promise to a community safe to make?
head: The six questions
speak: The people who do not work for me decide my timetable. I map them by power and interest and give each an owner in my company. I keep a register of every concern in their own words and every promise we have made, with the next contact date. I treat every safety concern as evidence and answer it in writing: Rule 73. I price what stakeholders can do. A six-month appeal costs carry, escalation and return at once, about 700,000 dollars on a hypothetical project, against an engagement budget of 185,000. Neighbours can stop work through private rights even when every permit is in order, so I offer condition surveys and monitoring. I follow the notice and consultation rules exactly, because defective process makes an approval vulnerable. And I promise only what has measurable terms, a cost in the budget and a mechanism behind it.
terms: Commitments register — a single record of every promise made to any stakeholder, with its authority, cost, trigger and owner.
Condition survey — a documented inspection of an adjoining building before and after works, to establish what damage, if any, the works caused.
Defective process — a failure to follow required notice or consultation steps, which can make an approval open to challenge.

hostile.q: Your site manager told neighbours you would make a generous contribution to the park. How much is it, and is it in the budget?
hostile.a: It is not in the budget, and it was not authorised. I will write to the neighbours this week to correct it: we have not agreed a park contribution, and if we propose one it will come with a figure, a date and a condition. Internally, no one makes a commitment to a stakeholder unless it is authorised and entered in the register first. If after talking to the community we decide a contribution is worth making, it will go into the pro forma before it goes into a letter.
